suggestions.rationale: Fecal incontinence is frequently associated with full-thickness rectal prolapse, and prospective cohort evidence shows that continence can improve after prolapse correction, particularly after ventral rectopexy. This supports a prolapse-related continence pathway when fecal incontinence is objectively and clinically documented in temporal and anatomic association with the prolapse; it does not establish that rectal prolapse is the sole cause of every continence disorder, because sphincter injury, pelvic-floor dysfunction, neuropathy, stool consistency, prior surgery, and other anorectal disease may independently contribute.

pathwayIntelligence.causalChain: Documented full-thickness rectal prolapse with pelvic-floor/anorectal dysfunction → impaired continence mechanism when present → clinically confirmed fecal incontinence compatible with the prolapse and individual anorectal findings.
developmentQuestions: Is full-thickness rectal prolapse objectively documented, and what are its severity, duration, and reducibility?
Is fecal incontinence clinically characterized by frequency, type, severity, and functional impact rather than inferred from the prolapse diagnosis alone?
What do anorectal examination, manometry, endoanal imaging, defecography, or other applicable testing show about sphincter function and pelvic-floor anatomy?
Did continence symptoms begin or worsen with the prolapse, and did they improve after successful prolapse repair if treatment occurred?
Which competing causes, including obstetric or surgical sphincter injury, neuropathy, diarrhea, inflammatory disease, medication effects, or other pelvic-floor disorders, should be addressed?
issuesToResolve: Fecal incontinence is common in rectal prolapse but may be multifactorial; the individual record must connect the continence deficit to the prolapse rather than assume a sole cause.
Anorectal anatomy, sphincter function, chronology, treatment response, and competing continence disorders require case-specific colorectal evaluation.

evidenceGaps: Colorectal examination or imaging confirming full-thickness rectal prolapse
Clinical characterization of fecal incontinence severity and chronology
Anorectal functional/anatomic testing when clinically indicated
Pre- and post-repair continence findings when prolapse surgery occurred
Colorectal opinion addressing competing sphincter, pelvic-floor, neurologic, stool-consistency, and surgical causes

sourceReferences.citation: Long-term impact of full-thickness rectal prolapse treatment on fecal incontinence. PMID 25869649
sourceReferences.note: Prospective single-center cohort of 145 patients with full-thickness rectal prolapse found fecal incontinence was frequent before treatment and that continence improvement was associated with ventral rectopexy compared with other operative or medical management. Supports an individual prolapse-associated continence pathway and treatment-response development, not automatic sole-cause attribution.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 25869649; abstract: prospective database of 145 full-thickness rectal-prolapse patients; 96% had fecal incontinence before treatment; continence improvement associated with ventral rectopexy
